video.title: The Most Overlooked $3K/Day Side Hustle Anyone Can Start (with $0)

summary: Heather describes building a seasonal porch pumpkin delivery and decorating business in the Dallas–Fort Worth area, from her first season to a much larger operation. Customers choose from fixed packages, with optional design and end-of-season pickup; she says social media and follow-up help bring in orders. The work depends on sourcing, storing, moving and arranging pumpkins, with drivers and designers helping at scale. Chris also pitches the idea to viewers and discusses pricing, customer acquisition and general business lessons.

speakers.name: Heather
speakers.description: Porch pumpkin business owner in the Dallas–Fort Worth area.

ideas.name: Porch pumpkin delivery and decorating
ideas.one_liner: Sell seasonal pumpkin packages for home porches, with optional setup and end-of-season pickup.
ideas.business_model: Seasonal one-off package sales, design add-ons, custom packages and optional pickup fees.
ideas.customer: Homeowners in the Dallas–Fort Worth area who want a decorated fall porch, including people hosting a party or looking for a particular style or colorway.
ideas.problem: Customers want a festive porch display but may not want to source, move, arrange or later dispose of the pumpkins themselves.
ideas.offer: Deliver a fixed package of pumpkins; customers can arrange them themselves or pay for design and setup. Some packages include design. Customers can also choose a custom package or pay for end-of-season pickup, when the pumpkins are taken to a pig farm.

pricing.model: One-off seasonal package pricing with optional add-ons.

price_points.label: Oh My Gourd package, includes design
Design for package three or four

pricing.notes: Heather says 95% of package three and four clients add design. She says 90% of package three customers choose pickup. The Oh My Gourd package has three colorways and includes design.

acquisition_channels.details: Heather posts porch displays on Instagram, follows current formats such as carousels and Reels, and adjusts content to what she sees performing well.

ideas.delivery: Heather initially sourced and moved pumpkins herself, drove them to homes and designed displays. At scale, pumpkins are bought from farms, stored in warehouse space, loaded onto trailers and delivered along routes. Drivers bring a truck and trailer, with dump trailers used for pickup; designers are paid per design and drivers hourly. Some packages are delivered without setup so customers can arrange the pumpkins themselves. Pickup orders are taken to a pig farm.
unit_economics_claims: Heather reports 50% profit margin in the first season, when she personally drove, unloaded and designed.
Heather says her current percentage margins are expected to be 50% to 55%.
Chris estimates a first season could bring $30,000 to $40,000 in sales and roughly $10,000 to $20,000 net profit; these are hypothetical projections.
Heather says six package three orders represent about $3,600 in revenue and take about 2.5 to 3 hours to deliver.
Heather estimates roughly $300 profit on one package three design job.
tools: Instagram for content, comments and boosted posts.
QuickBooks for sending invoices in the first season.
Venmo and online credit-card payment for collecting payment.
Pumpkin farms and produce suppliers for sourcing.
Warehouse space and cooler storage for inventory.
Trailers, including dump trailers, for delivery and pickup.
Forklift and wheelbarrow for moving pumpkins.
ideas.startup_cost: No startup amount is stated. Heather says a low-cost start could use a driver with a trailer and covered outdoor storage. The business still requires buying pumpkins; her later operation also has warehouse space, a forklift, trailers and umbrella insurance.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Heather says her phone began receiving orders on the third day of business. The exact time to first paid order is not stated; she says she started her first season on September 27 and sent invoices after the day's designs.

acquisition.how: Agents could schedule posts, adapt content formats and manage paid targeting. The transcript's approach also depends on creating visual content and personally replying to comments and following up with leads. Responding to inbound enquiries is distinct from unsolicited messaging.

onboarding.how: Fixed packages simplify choice and could be presented through an online form. The transcript describes sending invoices after collecting customer information, but does not describe automated order intake.

delivery.how: Pumpkins must be sourced, loaded, transported and physically arranged at each home. Drivers and designers perform the physical work.

billing.how: Online card payment and Venmo reduce payment friction, but Heather describes manually sending invoices. An agent could prepare invoices and reconcile payments with routine human checks.

support.how: Agents could answer standard package questions and provide order updates. Choosing a package, custom requests, delivery issues and seasonal inventory decisions still need human oversight.

uk_applicability.notes: The seasonal home-decoration service could be adapted to the UK, but the transcript's model is based on the Dallas–Fort Worth market, its homes and its supply routes. A UK operator would need local pumpkin suppliers, UK pricing and a route area suited to local housing and demand.

risks: Demand is concentrated around the fall and Halloween season, so revenue and workload are seasonal.
Delivery, setup and pickup require physical labor, vehicles and reliable seasonal staff.
Pumpkins require storage and can spoil or be damaged; buying too many can create surplus, while buying too few can mean turning customers away.
Long delivery routes can consume time and vehicle capacity; the transcript advises putting a price on serving farther-away areas.
The reported margins and sales are self-reported and may not generalize to a new market or operator.
Custom packages require more time to cost and may complicate operations; Heather sets a high minimum for them.

tactics.name: Use fixed packages to reduce buyer friction
steps: Offer a short menu of package sizes instead of asking every customer to invent a display.
Include a self-arrange option for customers who want delivery without setup.
Offer design as a $75 add-on for packages three and four.
Set a high minimum for custom packages so extra estimating time is worth taking on.

quote.text: But if you're saying choose this, this this or this, then they kind of they have a good direction, right?
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Build demand with current Instagram formats
steps: Watch which Instagram formats are currently performing and adapt the content mix.
Use porch photos and short videos to show the finished displays.
Boost posts to specific zip codes when paid promotion is useful.
Be ready to reply to comments soon after posting.

quote.text: And then also reals like so you have to follow what Instagram algorithm is putting out there.
quote.speaker: Heather

tactics.name: Follow up personally with inbound leads
steps: Treat an enquiry as a lead, not a confirmed order.
Reply to people who comment or message and ask for the information needed to place an order.
Remind interested customers if a promised photo or order detail has not arrived.
After an email blast, follow up one to one with people who have not ordered.

quote.text: You have to follow up with them. I mean, especially as a brand new entrepreneur, you need to follow up and make sure like, "Oh, coming back to make sure that I can help you place your order."
quote.speaker: Heather

tactics.name: Start with a small live test and keep selling
steps: Start before the peak season and collect orders early; Heather says she now starts collecting in July.
Use a few early homes to learn the delivery and design process.
Say yes to viable orders outside the immediate neighborhood, while putting a dollar amount on the added distance.

quote.text: Get three homes under your belt. You know, I started September 27th.
quote.speaker: Chris Koerner

tactics.name: Scale delivery with separate driver and designer roles
steps: Bring in a driver with a truck and trailer so the owner can serve more than a few homes at once.
Pay drivers hourly and designers by the design.
Ask customers who arrange their own displays to share a photo; Heather says she hired a designer after seeing one customer's work.

quote.text: And I even found like two designers that could help me in that first year.
quote.speaker: Heather

tactics.name: Match sourcing method to volume
steps: Use accessible suppliers such as nurseries or produce distributors when starting small.
As volume grows, buy directly from farms to get the quantity and variety needed.
Plan inventory to avoid running out, while keeping storage and surplus disposal in mind.

quote.text: The real secret is buying as many pumpkins as you need for your season. And so, the more pumpkins you need, then you can get them direct from farmers.
quote.speaker: Heather

tactics.name: Use a waitlist to fill late-season routes
steps: Track demand after the published delivery schedule fills.
Check the waitlist and add route days when inventory and crew capacity allow.
Heather says she planned a full route day on October 16 after the schedule was already through October 15.

quote.text: We'll look at that weight list and we'll just pull additional trailers at the end of the season.
quote.speaker: Heather

evidence_quality.rationale: Heather describes her own operation with specific package prices, sales, margins, staffing and delivery processes. The figures are self-reported, several are estimates, and Chris adds hypothetical projections; the video does not show independent records.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Chris promotes his podcast and asks viewers to subscribe and refer guests. Heather mentions her business classes, but the transcript does not detail their sales.
